theory.overview: Lexical analysis is the first phase of compilation—transforming raw source code into a stream of meaningful tokens. Think of it as the compiler's 'reading' phase: it scans characters, groups them into logical units (tokens), and discards whitespace and comments. Every programming language starts here, from Python to JavaScript to C++. Understanding tokenization helps you write better code, debug syntax errors, and even build your own domain-specific languages.

sections.title: What is a Token?
sections.content: A token is the smallest unit of meaning in source code. Just like words in a sentence, tokens carry semantic value. Examples include: keywords (`if`, `while`, `return`), identifiers (`myVariable`, `calculateSum`), operators (`+`, `==`, `->`), literals (`42`, `
`, `3.14`), and delimiters (`(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `;`). The lexer recognizes patterns using regular expressions or finite automata, grouping characters into these categories.
keyPoints: Tokens are the 'words' of programming languages
Each token has a type (keyword, identifier, operator, etc.)
Whitespace is typically discarded during tokenization
Comments are stripped out and don't become tokens

sections.title: The Tokenization Process
sections.content: Tokenization follows a systematic pipeline: 1) Read source code character by character, 2) Recognize patterns using rules, 3) Create token objects with type and value, 4) Handle errors for unrecognized characters. The lexer uses lookahead when needed—for example, distinguishing `=` (assignment) from `==` (equality) requires peeking at the next character. Keywords are typically checked before identifiers, so `while` becomes a keyword token, not an identifier.

sections.title: Finite State Machines
sections.content: Lexers are often implemented as Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)—state machines where each state represents what we're currently reading. We start in an 'initial' state. Seeing a letter transitions to 'identifier' state. Seeing a digit after that stays in 'identifier' (for variables like `var1`). Seeing an operator character transitions to 'operator' state. This formal approach ensures no ambiguity and enables efficient O(n) tokenization where n is source code length.
keyPoints: Each state handles specific character patterns
States transition based on input characters

sections.title: Handling Edge Cases
sections.content: Real-world lexers face complex scenarios: string literals with escape sequences (`"hello\nworld"`), multi-line comments that need nesting, heredocs in languages like Python and Ruby, number formats (hex `0xFF`, binary `0b1010`, scientific `1.5e-10`). A robust lexer needs state tracking for string interpolation and proper error recovery—if an unclosed string is detected, the lexer should report the line and column where it started.

examples.explanation: String with newline escape - lexer processes \n as single newline character
Some languages support nested block comments

keyConcepts.name: Maximal Munch Rule
keyConcepts.description: When multiple token patterns match, choose the longest match. `>>=` is one operator, not `>` followed by `>=`.

keyConcepts.name: Token Classification
keyConcepts.description: Keywords are reserved identifiers. Contextual keywords (like `async` in some languages) require special handling.

keyConcepts.name: Lexer Generator
keyConcepts.description: Tools like Lex, Flex, ANTLR generate optimized DFAs from regex-based token specifications.

keyConcepts.name: Error Recovery
keyConcepts.description: Good lexers skip invalid characters, report errors with line/column info, and continue tokenizing.

complexity.spaceComplexity: $O(1)$ for DFA state, $O(k)$ for $k$ tokens output

steps.title: Initialize Lexer State
steps.description: Set position to start of source, initialize empty token list, prepare keyword lookup table.

steps.title: Skip Whitespace
steps.description: Advance past spaces, tabs, newlines. Track line/column for error reporting.

steps.title: Identify Token Type
steps.description: Check current character: letter → identifier/keyword, digit → number, quote → string, special char → operator/delimiter.

steps.title: Extract Token Value
steps.description: Consume characters until pattern breaks. For identifiers: letters, digits, underscores. Apply maximal munch.

steps.title: Create Token Object
steps.description: Package type, value, line, column into token. Keywords take precedence over identifiers.

steps.title: Repeat or Terminate
steps.description: Continue from step 2 until end of input. Emit EOF token when complete.

practiceProblems.title: Tokenize Simple Expression
practiceProblems.explanation: Each distinct element becomes a token. The variable x, assignment operator, numbers, and plus operator are separate tokens.

practiceProblems.title: Identify Keywords vs Identifiers
practiceProblems.explanation: `if` and `return` are keywords. `while_true` is an identifier (underscore makes it one word, different from keyword `while`).

practiceProblems.title: String with Escapes
practiceProblems.explanation: Tokens: print(identifier), ((delimiter), "Hello\nWorld"(string), )(delimiter), ;(delimiter). The \n escape becomes part of the string's value, not separate tokens.
hints: The string is ONE token with processed escapes

practiceProblems.title: Multi-Character Operators
practiceProblems.explanation: Multi-char operators >=, &&, != are single tokens (maximal munch). Not > followed by =, or & followed by &.

practiceProblems.title: Number Formats
practiceProblems.explanation: Different numeric literals have different prefixes and formats. The lexer recognizes each pattern.

practiceProblems.title: Comment Handling
practiceProblems.description: How many tokens from: `x = 5; // set x to 5\ny = 10;`
practiceProblems.explanation: Tokens: x, =, 5, ;, y, =, 10, ;. The // comment and everything after it on that line is discarded. Newline ends the comment.
hints: // is line comment to end of line
Newline ends comment, not a token itself

practiceProblems.title: Complex Expression
practiceProblems.explanation: Each operator, identifier, parenthesis, and semicolon is a separate token. Parentheses create clear grouping.
hints: Each operator is its own token
Identifiers include result, a, b, c, d, e

practiceProblems.title: Lexer Complexity
practiceProblems.description: What is the time complexity of lexical analysis for n characters of source code?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each character is examined a constant number of times (typically once, sometimes twice for lookahead). Linear scan through the input.

practiceProblems.title: Ambiguity Resolution
practiceProblems.description: In a language where `>>` is right-shift and `>=` is greater-equal, how should `>>=` be tokenized?
practiceProblems.explanation: Maximal munch rule: longest match wins. >>= is 3 chars, >> is 2, >= is 2, > is 1. The 3-char operator >>= (right-shift-assign) is chosen.

practiceProblems.title: Line Continuation
practiceProblems.description:
Python uses `\` for line continuation. How many tokens: `x = 1 \\
    + 2`?
practiceProblems.answer: 4 tokens: x, =, 1, +, 2 simplified to x, =, 3 (but actually x, =, 1, +, 2 -> 5 tokens)
practiceProblems.explanation: The backslash-newline is removed by lexer before tokenization. Result: x, =, 1, +, 2 (5 tokens). The values combine at parse/execution time, not lex.
hints: Newline after \ is not a token separator
Operators and values remain separate tokens

minigame.title: Token Master
minigame.description: Test your lexical analysis skills! Race against time to identify correct tokens from code snippets. Learn to recognize patterns and apply maximal munch.
instructions: Identify each token and its type
Click tokens in order to classify them

visualizer.description: Watch how a lexer processes source code in real-time. See characters transform into tokens, observe state transitions, and understand maximal munch in action.
